People who buy their food pre-made, often have no idea how cheap food actually can be, if they were it to prepare it themselves.

Where I live, a pizza at a fast food establishment is usually at least 5€, a frozen one at a supermarket at least 1€, while one I made myself can be as cheap 0.50€.

I actually made around 35 small pizzas (7-8 inches diameter) yesterday and froze them, since I'm a big fan of preparing my own food well in advance. They have around 300 calories each and only cost between 0.14-0.24€ each, depending on the topping.

Granted, preparing your own food takes time, but that's literally one of the most basic human tasks that everyone should be able to perform.
Your pizza sounds amazing. What's your recipe? ~300 calories is perfect for a serving!

For the dough I used 500g plain flour, 7g dry yeast, 17 ml olive oil, 8g salt, 300ml warm water. I multiplied these amounts by 6 to get a bigger amount (4.8kg instead of just 800g dough).

Mix all the dry ingredients, then add oil and warm (not hot) water, knead for at least 10 minutes and let it rise for at least one hour in a warm spot (not hot) while covered with a wet towel or cling wrap.

For the sauce I cooked 6 cans (400ml each) of diced tomatoes, 150g of tomato paste, 500g of onions, 25 ml of olive oil and some garlic for a few hours while stirring regularly, until it was a really thick sauce (2.4kg from 3.05kg ingredients) and used a blender to make it a bit smoother.

Then I added salt and a fuckload of herbs, about 50% dried oregano, 35% dried basil and 15% dried thyme. I didn't measure them, but I probably used 2 cups of herbs. It's important to add the herbs at the very end when the sauce is otherwise finished and not boiling anymore, otherwise they'll lose their flavour really fast.

I know that the sauce is really labour intensive, but it's the most important part of the entire pizza for me. You could probably substitute some canned tomatoes for tomato paste to thicken it up, instead of boiling it for so long. Since it's important to not have too much water in the sauce (otherwise the dough will soak it up), I like to go all the way.

When the dough and sauce are done, I let the sauce cool down a few minutes, while seperating the dough into pieces of 100g each (234 calories). Make sure not to do this with the entire dough if you're making a big amount, since the small balls of dough might start to dry out, I only did about 10 at a time and kept the rest of the dough covered when I wasn't using it.

Dust the pieces of dough in a bit of flour, I then carefully pull them apart, since this doesn't press the CO2 the yeast created outside like a rolling pin would, resulting in a better rise in the ofen. This takes some practise, so use a rolling pin (on a surface dusted with flour) if you'd like to. If you use a rolling pin, your pizza will be much more evenly flattened and larger in diameter.

I spread a layer of about 20g tomato sauce (19 calories) on every pizza, which was enough since the sauce was really thick and strong. Then I added one or two toppings (20g onions(8cal)/ 20g mushrooms(4cal)/17g ham(17cal)/ 8g salami(25cal)) and topped it off with 10g of sliced gouda (37 calories/ cheaper than shredded cheese, cheapest one available and easy to portion), which was enough since I didn't use a rolling pin.

If you plan on freezing the pizza to eat at a later date, place the dough (before putting anything on top) on a sheet of baking paper (I used aluminium foil, but the bottom didn't cook well enough), put everything on the pizza, then fold the edges of baking paper up and cover everything in a layer or two of cling wrap. Make sure to put some flour between the dough and baking paper, otherwise it might stick to the pizza after baking.

I didn't take any pictures, but I might upload a picture of one of the pizzas later.
